freezecore's MGRS grid is the star of this package. It's a fast, easy to use grid metadata standard that allows working with multimodal raster data.

## Why a common grid

When doing deep learning with satellite-based Earth Observation data, this often means stacking rasters that were never meant to be stacked. A Sentinel-1
backscatter scene, a Sentinel-2 optical composite, a DEM, and a glacier outline arrive in different coordinate reference systems, at different resolutions,
cut into different tiles. Before any of it reaches a model, it has to be resampled onto
something shared. `MGRSGrid` is that fixed target.

In addition, more and more projects do global scale analysis. Where you could previously define a single Area of Interest
with single projection, things break down once you go global. Handling different area of interests with different projections is what this grid system is set out to simplify.



## Why MGRS

This grid isn't defining a new standard. Instead, as the name suggests, it implements the [Military Grid Reference
System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Grid_Reference_System). This has the following advantages:

**It is an established standard.** MGRS is a well-specified subdivision of UTM with
decades of use. Nothing here needs inventing or defending.

**Sentinel-2 already uses it.** Copernicus distributes Sentinel-2 products on MGRS 100 km
squares (`T32TMS` and friends). When ingesting Sentinel-2 data, this means no quality-loosing resampling is needed.

**Its squares are metric and axis-aligned.** Each MGRS square lives in a UTM zone, so
distances are in metres and the grid is aligned to the projection axes. A 10 m pixel is
10 m, not a varying fraction of a degree.

### Where freezecore's grid differs

Compared to Sentinel-2's tiling grid, freezecore comes with two main advantages:


**10 × 10 km squares for targeted downloading** Instead of working with 100 km × 100 km like Sentinel-2, 10 km × 10 km squares allow to specifically match an area of interest. This allows for targeted download of raster data. It speeds up download speed and reduces storage demand. Ideal for global scale analysis of scattered AOIs, like glaciers.

**No overlap.** Sentinel-2 tiles come with a wasteful[^1]overlap. freezecore's squares tile their UTM zone edge to
edge, storing each location only once.


[^1]: Bauer-Marschallinger, B., & Falkner, K. (2023). Wasting petabytes: A survey of the
Sentinel-2 UTM tiling grid and its spatial overhead. *ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and
Remote Sensing*, 202, 682–690. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2023.07.015>

### A specification, not a dataset

`MGRSGrid` holds no pixels. It is a grid *specification* — a rule
for deriving, from an MGRS code, exactly one CRS, one affine transform, and one array
shape. Two pipelines that never exchange a file will still produce byte-aligned rasters
if they both resample onto the square named `32TMS35`.

## Building a grid for an AOI

Construct a grid by handing it an area of interest in WGS84. Any shapely geometry works -- from a single polygon to a `geopandas.GeoSeries` containing thousands of geometries.

The AOI below deliberately straddles 6° E, the boundary between UTM zones 31 and 32, so
the grid has to span two zones:

```{python}
from shapely import box

from freezecore.mgrs import MGRSGrid

# Geneva, Switzerland
aoi = box(5.8, 46.0, 6.5, 46.4)
grid = MGRSGrid(aoi)

len(grid)
```

`to_geodataframe()` materialises the grid as a WGS84 `GeoDataFrame`, one row per square:

```{python}
gdf = grid.to_geodataframe()
gdf.head()
```

Each row carries the MGRS code, the UTM zone and hemisphere it belongs to, the EPSG code
of that zone's CRS, and the square's south-west corner in UTM metres. Note the `epsg`
column holds two distinct values here:

```{python}
gdf.groupby(["zone", "epsg"]).size()
```

This is the point that a single-CRS grid cannot express. The squares west of 6° E are
defined in EPSG:32631 and those east of it in EPSG:32632, and neither is a
reprojection of the other — they are separate metric grids that happen to abut.

## Seeing the grid

Plotting the squares over a basemap makes the two-zone structure obvious. Because the
zone 31 and zone 32 grids are each axis-aligned in *their own* projection, they appear
rotated relative to one another once drawn in a common CRS:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "10 km grid squares over Geneva, Switzerland, coloured by UTM zone. The zone 31 squares (left) are visibly rotated against the zone 32 squares, because each grid is axis-aligned in its own projection."
#| warning: false
import contextily as cx
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
import pyproj

WEB_MERCATOR = pyproj.CRS(3857)

# Web Mercator, so the squares and the basemap tiles agree
squares = gdf.to_crs(WEB_MERCATOR)
aoi_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[aoi], crs=4326).to_crs(WEB_MERCATOR)

zone_colors = {31: "tab:blue", 32: "tab:red"}
alpha = 0.2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
for zone, color in zone_colors.items():
    squares[squares.zone == zone].plot(
        ax=ax, facecolor=color, alpha=alpha, edgecolor=color, linewidth=1.0
    )
aoi_gdf.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--")

cx.add_basemap(ax, source=cx.providers.CartoDB.Positron, crs=WEB_MERCATOR, attribution_size=6)
ax.legend(
    handles=[
        *(Patch(facecolor=c, alpha=alpha, edgecolor=c, label=f"UTM zone {z}")
          for z, c in zone_colors.items()),
        Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor="k", linestyle="--", label="AOI"),
    ],
    loc="lower right",
    frameon=True,
);
```

## A grid square is a GeoBox

Indexing the grid returns an `MGRSGeoBox`, which is a subclass of
[`odc.geo.geobox.GeoBox`](https://odc-geo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/intro-geobox.html):

```{python}
from odc.geo.geobox import GeoBox

square = grid[0]
square, isinstance(square, GeoBox)
```

That inheritance is the whole design. A `GeoBox` is the minimal complete description of a
georeferenced raster — CRS, affine transform, and shape — which is exactly the three
things a resampling call needs:

```{python}
print(f"mgrs_code:  {square.mgrs_code}")
print(f"crs:        {square.crs}")
print(f"shape:      {square.shape}")
print(f"resolution: {square.resolution}")
print(f"transform:\n{square.transform}")
```

Everything `odc-geo` offers comes along, including the bounding box in native and
geographic coordinates:

```{python}
square.boundingbox
```

```{python}
square.geographic_extent.boundingbox
```

…and a rich HTML representation, which renders the square on a map in Jupyter and Quarto:

```{python}
square
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Derived boxes are plain GeoBoxes

`odc-geo` operations that return a *new* box — `pad()`, `zoom_out()`, `to_crs()`,
slicing — return a plain `GeoBox`, not an `MGRSGeoBox`, and so carry no `mgrs_code`:

```{python}
type(square.pad(10)).__name__
```

This is intended. A padded or reprojected box is no longer the square that the MGRS code
names, so it should not claim that identity.
:::

## Iterating and slicing

`MGRSGrid` behaves like a sequence of squares. Iterating yields `MGRSGeoBox` instances,
which is the usual way to drive per-square work:

```{python}
for square in grid[:3]:
    print(f"{square.mgrs_code}  {square.crs}  {square.geographic_extent.boundingbox.left:.3f}°E")
```

Slicing returns a new `MGRSGrid` rather than a list, so filters compose:

```{python}
len(grid[:20])
```

## Starting from a code

When the square is already known — from a filename, a database, or an earlier run — there
is no need to build a grid at all. `MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs()` reconstructs it from the code
alone:

```{python}
from freezecore.mgrs import MGRSGeoBox

MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs("32TMS35")
```

This is what makes the grid a specification rather than a dataset. The code is the only
thing that needs storing or transmitting; the geometry is derivable.

To go from a code to just its CRS, use `mgrs_to_crs()`, which parses the code without any
grid construction:

```{python}
from freezecore.mgrs import mgrs_to_crs

mgrs_to_crs("32TMS35")
```

## Choosing a resolution

`resolution` is the pixel size in metres and defaults to 10 m, matching Sentinel-1 GRD and
Sentinel-2's 10 m bands. It must divide 10 km evenly, so the square is always a whole
number of pixels:

```{python}
for res in (10.0, 20.0, 100.0):
    gb = MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs("32TMS35", resolution=res)
    print(f"{res:>5.0f} m -> {gb.shape}")
```

The square's footprint never changes with resolution — only how finely it is sampled.
That means a 10 m layer and a 20 m layer of the same square remain exactly co-registered,
with an integer scale factor between them.

## Zone boundaries

Within a UTM zone, the squares tile the zone edge to edge with no gaps and no double coverage. Across a zone boundary that no longer holds. Each zone's grid is built independently and squares that span span into the next zone are kept to make sure there are no holes in the coverage.
However, this means that a square in zone 31 and a square in zone 32 can cover overlapping ground. For this AOI —
chosen to straddle a boundary, so close to a worst case — the duplication is:

```{python}
LAEA = pyproj.CRS(3035)
areas = gdf.to_crs(LAEA)

covered = areas.union_all().area
summed = areas.area.sum()

print(f"sum of squares: {summed / 1e6:8.0f} km²")
print(f"ground covered: {covered / 1e6:8.0f} km²")
print(f"duplication:    {(summed - covered) / covered:8.1%}")
```

This redundancy is inherent to any UTM-based grid when working across zone boundaries. Due to the small footprint of the squares, the overlap can be kept to a minimum.
